The August CPI print (due before the Sep 15-16 meeting, which carries fresh projections) is the named swing factor. Do not read the soft July CPI/payrolls pair as cut-risk — nothing is priced there.

active_narratives.title: Hyperscaler AI Capex Bubble Concerns: Datacenter $1.7T by 2030 vs. ROI Validation Risk
active_narratives.summary: Hyperscaler AI capex has outgrown the original $1.7T-by-2030 framing so decisively that its author retired it: Dell'Oro nearly DOUBLED its data-center capex forecast to >$3T by 2030 on Aug 18, 2026 (from $1.7T in January, newly counting the AI-specialized cloud segment). The Big Four alone guide to roughly $730B in 2026 (Alphabet $195-205B, Amazon ~$220B after raising from ~$200B on Jul 30, Microsoft $175B for CALENDAR 2026, restated from ~$190B on a useful-life reclass with spend unchanged, Meta $130-145B after narrowing from $125-145B on Jul 29 — a $5B floor raise, per the release verbatim) and analysts project ~$1T in 2027 (a circulating '$1.15T' is Morgan Stanley's figure INCLUDING SpaceX as a new hyperscaler — not like-for-like). Semiconductor supply chains benefit directly, but ROI-validation and financing-cost concerns have intensified as the numbers grew — a WSJ report (~Aug 18) put ~$3T of off-balance-sheet, mostly AI-related commitments across nine top tech firms.
active_narratives.thesis: AI infrastructure spending remains a strong tailwind for semis, memory, optics and power infrastructure, but multiple-compression risk emerges if capex growth decelerates or demand does not materialise. The Q2 2026 print season is now COMPLETE and it resolved in favour of continuation: all four reported by 30 July and none guided down — Alphabet RAISED to $195-205B on 22 July flagging a significant further increase in 2027, Meta narrowed to $130-145B (from $125-145B — a $5B floor raise) on 29 July, Microsoft restated calendar-2026 capex to $175B on a useful-life reclass (buildings 15-to-25 years, effective FY2027) with spend unchanged, and Amazon RAISED to ~$220B on 30 July. Read the Amazon raise as a different kind: it was attributed to HIGHER MEMORY COSTS — paying more for the same capacity, not buying more — so it is a weaker demand signal than a unit-driven raise and it transmits to memory vendors rather than along the whole chain, though Jassy said Amazon still will not have enough capacity for 2026 demand. The live constraint has shifted from willingness to spend toward the cost of funding it — the ~$12B El Paso datacenter bond (precisely: $12.55B of notes at a 7.5% coupon priced Jul 27 by the BlackRock-led JV holdco, BlackRock 80% / Meta 20%) and Amazon's $25B July issue (order book peaked ~$62B, final ~$41B, with an extra-yield concession — cooler than its March deal) are the anchors, and Alphabet's debut A$5.5B Kangaroo bond (Aug 19) priced its 20-year tranche near 7% — long-dated money for an AAA-class issuer now costs ~7% in AUD. Rates compound this: the Fed is priced hold-versus-hike rather than easing (Sep 16: ~32% hike / ~68% hold / 0% cut, with the Jul-29 minutes showing 'several' favoring an immediate hike), which is a duration headwind for capex-intensive mega-caps. A first guide-down or 'digestion' framing from any major hyperscaler would be a cluster-wide thesis-break check, not a single-ticker event.

active_narratives.title: US-China Semiconductor Supply Chain Reshaping: Tariffs vs. Foundry Demand
active_narratives.summary: US-China technology restrictions continue to reshape semiconductor supply chains, but the direction is mixed rather than uniformly escalating. ASML's standing 2030 ambition is EUR 44-60B revenue set at its Nov 2024 Investor Day and never revised — though the FY26 guide midpoint (~EUR 44B) already touches its floor — and Intel's 18A is in volume production, with High-NA EUV dual-qualified on a subset of 18A layers in Oregon (High-NA-DEPENDENT high-volume manufacturing is a 2027/14A story, not a current fact). Onshoring economics support equipment and memory capex. China's materials levers are NOT all retaliation: the helium export prohibition (in force since Jul 10, open-ended) is GLOBAL in scope and driven by the Qatar supply shock — MOFCOM says on record it targets no country — while the genuine trade-war channel is the suspension cliffs: rare-earth/magnet measures lapse 2026-11-10 and Ga/Ge/antimony 2026-11-27, both snapping back by default; note the ban on dual-use exports to US MILITARY end users and the tungsten/indium/rare-earth measures of early 2025 were never suspended, so 'controls are paused' is too broad.
active_narratives.thesis: Structural supply-chain tailwinds from US-China decoupling support the onshoring complex — Intel 18A and 14A, ASML EUV, Micron's >$250B cumulative US plan through 2035 (raised from ~$200B on Jul 9, 2026) — while elevated cost of capital constrains the multiple paid for that demand. The policy picture is two-directional and the 'officials speaking vs agencies acting' rule now needs a SPLIT: on Moonshot specifically it still holds (no designation, no docket), but the distillation/model-export lane has formal instruments — OSTP's NSTM-4 directive on adversarial distillation (Apr 23, 2026) and a BIS is-informed letter requiring licences for certain frontier US model exports including API access (Jun 12, 2026) — while open-WEIGHT models remain uncontrolled. The Hong Kong emergency order lapsed Jul 14 and MOFCOM tariff-cut consultations (~$30B each way) continue. The durable read stands: weight enacted measures (the November materials cliffs, existing licence regimes) over statements. On H200 exports to China the binding constraint is Beijing, not Washington — BIS has granted licences to 10+ Chinese firms but Beijing's posture is selective and NVIDIA recognizes zero China H200 revenue, excluding it from guidance entirely.

active_narratives.title: ECB Rate Hold Diverges from Fed Hawkish Pause: Euro Weakness Implication
active_narratives.summary: ECB held the deposit rate at 2.25% on Jul 23, 2026 after hiking 25bp on Jun 11 — its first hike since 2023 — with markets pricing a 25bp hike at the Sep 10 projection meeting at roughly 70-80%. The divergence has INVERTED: this is a tightening bias, not an easing cycle, and while the rate-LEVEL premium persists (Fed 3.50-3.75% vs ECB 2.25%), near-term policy direction now points opposite ways — ECB hiking as base case, Fed ~68% hold — which is what the euro is expressing: EUR/USD ~1.155 at the Aug 14 close (an eight-week high) with DXY ~99.6.
active_narratives.thesis: The ECB is in a tightening bias, not an easing one: 25bp on Jun 11 to a 2.25% deposit rate, held on Jul 23 with some governors questioning whether more was warranted (a 'unanimous' vote characterization is unverified — drop it). July was a non-projection meeting so the bar to move was structurally higher; Sep 10 carries fresh forecasts and is the live decision, with the July FINAL HICP confirmed at 2.9% (Aug 20 fetch) and the August flash ~Aug 31 as the last major input. Energy-driven inflation is the shared driver with the Fed, so the policy-RATE gap is narrowing even as near-term direction diverges — the euro-weakness-on-divergence leg is the part of this narrative most at risk of being wrong, and it is now measurably inverted. Eurozone data keeps supporting the hike case: Q2 GDP +0.4% QoQ / +1.0% YoY CONFIRMED UNREVISED at the Aug 14 second estimate (employment +0.1% QoQ), and July flash HICP 2.9% with core 2.5%, services 3.3% and energy 10.0% — services is the component the ECB actually watches. Global duration headwinds across developed markets still hold as a conclusion, but because everyone is tightening, not because the Fed is an outlier.

active_narratives.title: US-Iran Hormuz Blockade Escalation: Oil Supply Crisis Resurfaces
active_narratives.summary: US naval blockade of Iranian ports and the Hormuz disruption are INTACT as of Aug 22, 2026: the blockade was reimposed in mid-July (CENTCOM count now 64 vessels redirected, 3 disabled, 2 boarded — per Lloyd's List citing CENTCOM, Aug 19), the strait is closed to normal commercial transit (~10-11 ships/day — 73 in the week Aug 10-16 — vs ~100 pre-war, roughly -90%), and there is NO ceasefire and never was one in August: the Jun 17 memorandum's 60-day deal window formally EXPIRED Aug 17 with no deal, so 'US-Iran ceasefire expires' headlines are a framing garble, not a state change — the memorandum itself collapsed mid-July. The diplomatic picture DEGRADED this week: Lloyd's List calls US-Iran diplomacy 'effectively collapsed', the Iran-Oman managed-transit corridor track can no longer be described as a live channel, and escalation has shifted to the SANCTIONS lane — the UAE suspended all financial/economic transactions with Iran INDEFINITELY on Aug 19 (alleging Iranian missiles targeted maritime traffic; Iran denies), and Treasury Secretary Bessent announced a 'toughest sanctions in history' coordinated-isolation package with a news conference set for Mon Aug 24. WTI ~$86.5 on Aug 21 (Brent ~$93.4), a second consecutive weekly gain; April peak was $104.91.
active_narratives.thesis: The load-bearing tension has evolved: the premium is HEADLINE-REACTIVE and this week the headlines were all escalation — WTI rose from ~$81 (Aug 14) to ~$86.5 (Aug 21) on the deal-window expiry, the UAE embargo and the US sanctions-package announcements, so the premium is re-arming without any new physical change in the strait. Do not read falling crude as the strait reopening (it has not reopened), and do not read 'ceasefire expires' headlines as a state change (no operative ceasefire existed — the mid-July collapse already did the damage). Transmission legs that still apply: logistics cost inflation from rerouting and tanker diversions pressures semiconductor supply chains (ASML, TSM, MU); Russia/Ukraine strikes on Black Sea shipping (nine claimed in 24h ~Aug 21) add a second freight-risk theater. The rate leg: July CPI (Aug 12) landed in line and Sep 16 pricing sits ~32% hike / ~68% hold / 0% cut, but the Jul-29 FOMC minutes (released Aug 19) showed 'several' participants favoring an immediate hike and 'many' seeing tightening likely if inflation does not decline — an oil-driven inflation impulse feeds directly into that split; next markers are Warsh's Jackson Hole keynote Fri Aug 28 and the Monday Aug 24 sanctions news conference. Falsifiable both ways: resumed strikes or the sanctions package re-arm the premium further, while an ACTUAL reopening to normal transit -- not a permissioned corridor -- would be the first genuine supply improvement and has NOT happened.

active_narratives.title: Microsoft Azure AI Revenue Concentration: OpenAI 45% Backlog Dependency
active_narratives.summary: Microsoft's disclosed 45% OpenAI share of Azure backlog is a DECEMBER-quarter figure that has never been refreshed — do not quote it as current; the closest refresh is Hood's Q4 remark that commercial RPO grew +25% EXCLUDING OpenAI, with all sequential RPO growth from customers outside the frontier-model companies. The exclusivity unwind was TWO stages, not one late-April event: Microsoft's compute right-of-first-refusal ended Oct 28, 2025 (Microsoft blog, primary), and the residual Azure API exclusivity ended ~Apr 27, 2026 (REPORTED — trade-press convergence; GPT-5.5 appeared on Amazon Bedrock Apr 28), so OpenAI can now buy compute elsewhere. Q4 FY2026 printed Jul 29, 2026: commercial RPO $678B (+84% YoY) and Azure +43% constant currency, both ahead of the prior $627B/~40%.
active_narratives.thesis: Single-vendor concentration risk is real but has moved on two axes since this was written. With exclusivity fully unwound (ROFR Oct 2025, API exclusivity Apr 2026), the forward question is no longer lock-in but whether OpenAI-linked Azure consumption DECELERATES now that it can buy elsewhere — the cleaner read on calls is Azure growth ex-OpenAI, and the RPO-ex-OpenAI +25% disclosure is the first partial refresh of the concentration picture. Microsoft is also actively reducing the dependency with in-house MAI models — but the '89% cheaper than OpenAI' figure is Microsoft's own self-reported GPU-cost reduction for MAI-Voice-2-Flash in Dynamics 365 Contact Center ONLY, not API pricing and not portfolio-wide; do not generalize it. Capex is the swing factor: $175B restated for 2026 (from ~$190B — a useful-life reclass, spend unchanged, NOT a cut), with memory prices as the cost driver — a direct link to the memory-supercycle narrative, now confirmed from outside Microsoft by Amazon naming higher memory costs as the reason for its ~$200B to ~$220B raise on Jul 30. Two anchors here are stale and should not be reused: the 45% backlog share (December quarter, never refreshed) and the $1.7T-by-2030 capex figure, against Big-4 2026 guided capex of roughly $730B. US10Y is 4.64%, not 4.42%.

Market re-rating has NOT arrived: signal is CAUTION as of the Aug 21 report (eased from the Aug 5 AVOID), with external foundry traction the stated doubt — and the funding question resolved as equity: the offering closed at ~$23.0B gross (242,105,262 shares at $95, greenshoe exercised in full; '$20B' and '$24B' variants are the base deal and a garble respectively).
active_narratives.thesis: 18A milestone validates Intel's foundry roadmap and CHIPS Act investment, potentially shifting competitive landscape against TSMC. However, INTC remains signal-negative (CAUTION as of Aug 21, AVOID Aug 5-20) until the market reprices foundry competitiveness and demand visibility — the external customer book is still Fortinet on mature Intel 4 plus $293M of quarterly foundry revenue, with no new signing since Jul 21 (re-verified Aug 22); the US government sat out the offering, diluting its ~9.9% stake to ~9.5%, and the 'Tan bought another 105,000 shares' Aug 19 headlines re-run his Aug 14 Form 4 offering participation at $95, not a fresh open-market buy. Dated markers: director/officer lock-up expires ~Sep 9; 14A PDK 0.9 due October.

active_narratives.title: BigTech AI Strategy Divergence: GOOG TPU Upgrade vs MSFT/AMZN Caution
active_narratives.summary: Market differentiating BigTech AI exposure by structure rather than by any single day's rating: GOOG's in-house TPU stack, MSFT's OpenAI/Azure concentration, AMZN's capex load. Signal states across the three have churned repeatedly -- GOOG ran BUY to CAUTION to HOLD between June and late July -- so the durable content here is the structural split, not a signal triple that decays within days.
active_narratives.thesis: Divergence reflects structural AI strategy differences. GOOG benefits from owning its accelerator roadmap -- Ironwood GA, with 8th-gen Sunfish/Zebrafish only in select-customer preview and GA not until late 2027 -- and raised FY26 capex to $195-205B (NOT the '>=$180B' an earlier update recorded: $180-190B was the PRIOR guide). MSFT's OpenAI concentration is the most-cited risk but has softened -- the late-April rewrite ended cloud exclusivity and MSFT is shipping in-house models it says cut costs up to 89% -- and the 45% Azure-backlog share is a December-quarter figure never refreshed, so it should not be quoted as current. AMZN carries ~$220B FY26 capex (raised from ~$200B on 30 July, attributed to higher memory costs) against a genuine AWS reacceleration -- Q2 AWS grew 37% to $42.2B, its fastest since Q4 2021. The Jul 22-30 print window has now CLOSED and all three reported, so the June framing is superseded: the actuals show all three still raising or holding capex with none guiding down, and the divergence now runs on who funds it from operating cash and who is paying input-cost inflation for the same capacity.
